title: Castleton Private Egress & On‑Ramp Intake
topics: Egress IP whitelisting and NAT allocation
Cross-region data residency and region gating (EU)
DNS resolution / split-horizon and conditional forwarding
On-prem VPN vs Direct Connect / Transit gateway
KMS integration, audit logs, and cert management
summary: Initial technical intake to understand Castleton's private deployment constraints: they need private endpoints into Redwood, predictable egress IPs for partner whitelisting, EU data residency for certain models, split-horizon DNS for service discovery, and an on-prem fallback via Direct Connect. Redwood AE + SE outlined Private vs Dedicated tradeoffs and asked for IP ranges, timelines, and security artifacts.

transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-10-12
Start time: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Lena (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Dana (Castleton Head Infra), Ravi (Castleton Network Eng), Elena (Castleton Sec Arch)

Summary (auto): quick intake on private endpoints, egress IPs for partner whitelisting, region gating for EU models, and on-prem connectivity options.

00:00:00 - Lena: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Lena from Redwood inference, I'm AE on this account, with Marcus from our solutions team. quick intro?
00:00:08 - Dana: Hey all, Dana here, I run infrastructure at Castleton, we've got Ravi and Elena on to dig into network/security. thanks for doing this.
00:00:15 - Marcus: Hi, Marcus, SE. we'll try to map out options — Private endpoints, peering, transit gw, whatever fits your compliance needs.
00:00:30 - Ravi: Quick note - we have a hard requirement that outbound IPs to a 3rd party partner must be static/whitelisted. also some workloads must stay in eu-west-1.
00:00:42 - Lena: Great. that's common. can you confirm you want Redwood Private (VPC + private endpoints) or are you open to Dedicated?
00:00:53 - Dana: We're leaning Private — we need a controlled network path and our security team wants customer-managed VPC peering or PrivateLink. cost is secondary to compliance.
00:01:06 - Marcus: Ok. two high-level plumbing patterns: VPC peering/transit gateway which is straightforward but requires route management and might expose VPC-level connectivity; or PrivateLink/private endpoints (Privatelink) which gives you service endpoints in your VPC and restricts surface. both support private IPs but differ on DNS and cross-account routing.
00:01:30 - Elena: Follow up: with PrivateLink will we be able to preserve original client IPs for logging? partners need that. sometimes we lose source IP behind NAT.
00:01:40 - Marcus: Good question. Privatelink typically terminates at the interface endpoint — your egress will come from Redwood's NAT if you go out to partner endpoints we manage. for whitelisting we usually offer a static egress IP pool you can reference, or you can arrange egress from your side if you want egress to be on-prem.
00:01:59 - Ravi: So two things: static egress IPs from Redwood for partners OR set up routing so partner traffic goes via our on-prem? what's easier?
00:02:10 - Lena: For speed to pilot, many customers accept Redwood-provided static egress IPs (we publish a small range per deployment). long term you can force egress through your NAT with route table tweaks / proxy.
00:02:24 - Dana: Also we have strict zone constraints: EU-only for PII inference. we need to ensure model hosting and prompts stay in eu-west-1 region. does Redwood support region gating per workload?
00:02:36 - Marcus: Yes — we can pin model variants by region. Private deployment can be instantiated in eu-west-1. we support routing policies that route EU traffic to EU-hosted model instances. there is an ops step for multi-region setup but it's supported.
00:02:52 - Elena: Audit and KMS — we need to ensure all logs go to our log pipeline and KMS is customer-managed HSM ideally. is HSM/KMS supported for Private?
00:03:02 - Marcus: Customer-managed KMS is supported on Private — we integrate with your KMS for key wrapping. HSM on-prem can be handled with bring-your-own-key and we can add KMIP integration in some cases, but that will be engineering scope.
00:03:18 - Ravi: DNS — we use split-horizon DNS and conditional forwarding to resolve internal service names. how does Redwood recommend setting up DNS for endpoints?
00:03:27 - Marcus: Two options: 1) PrivateLink with interface endpoints and create a private hosted zone you point to the interface ENIs; or 2) for VPC peering / transit, you can configure conditional forwarding to Redwood's resolver in the peered VPC. note that peering doesn't support transitive DNS by default, so transit gw or Route53 resolver endpoints may be needed.
00:03:51 - Dana: We have AWS Route53 resolver endpoints in our VPC already. is that compatible?
00:03:56 - Marcus: Yes, you can use inbound/outbound endpoints on Route53 resolver to do conditional forwarding between your VPC and ours. that often gives the cleanest split-horizon behavior.
00:04:09 - Lena: I want to flag an operations note - for Private we ask for an initial IP allowlist for management (eg our control plane agents need to reach your API endpoints during install). we'll provide the exact ranges in the runbook.
00:04:23 - Ravi: What's the typical MTU and any fragmentation concerns? we run some encrypted tunnels and small MTU caused issues in the past.
00:04:30 - Marcus: Typical is 1500; if you have VPNs with 1400 effective MTU we can adjust. we haven't seen big problems but we do test with larger sequence lengths since model token payloads can be large. sometimes K V cache calls add to that.
00:04:47 - Elena: Security controls — SSO, RBAC, audit logs. we need SAML SSO and SCIM for provisioning, and fine-grained RBAC to restrict model ops.
00:04:57 - Lena: We support SAML SSO + SCIM and have role-based access control that integrates with your identity provider. audit logs can be shipped to your ingest (S3 or syslog) with 90-day retention by default; extended retention is an add-on.
00:05:12 - Dana: On the networking side, partner vendors will only accept a handful of static IPs. how small can the egress pool be?
00:05:20 - Marcus: We try to keep it concise — in many cases we can publish a /28 or /27 for egress for a Dedicated or Private deployment, but it depends on scale. we can check IP exhaustion requirements in our sizing stage.
00:05:35 - Ravi: If we go transit gateway and route through our NAT GW, does that mean partner traffic egresses from our own IPs?
00:05:42 - Marcus: Correct — if you want partner whitelisting to reference your NAT IPs, you'd route requests through your NAT by advertising routes via transit gw or Direct Connect. there is more routing to set up but it's doable.
00:05:55 - Dana: Is there a recommended approach when we have both EU and US data residency needs — like keep PII in EU but non-PII in US?
00:06:04 - Marcus: Yes, you'd map workloads to regions and pin models/instances. Redwood's smart routing can send requests to region-specific endpoints. the tricky part is ensuring the client side sets a flag or the routing policy uses source IP or tenant attribute; we discussed a couple of strategies in the doc I'll send.
00:06:20 - Ravi: Latency concerns — some of our ML features are latency sensitive. if we pin to EU instances that adds latency for US clients. any edge options?
00:06:29 - Lena: For latency-critical, Dedicated in a region near your users is best. Private can still be optimized with caching and local model variants. Redwood Optimize suggests quantization and batching profiles to reduce token latency.
00:06:43 - Elena: Compliance question: do you have SOC2 Type II and ISO attestation? we need to share that with our auditors.
00:06:50 - Lena: Yes SOC2 type II yes; ISO is roadmap for this quarter — I'll include the latest security pack and a statement of roadmap items.
00:06:59 - Dana: About certs and MTLS — we prefer mutual TLS for service-to-service auth. does Private support mutual TLS between our clients and the Redwood endpoint?
00:07:09 - Marcus: Mutual TLS is supported at the edge for Private endpoints; you can upload client certs to our provisioning flow and we validate them. for inter-service mTLS inside your VPC you'd manage those certs.
00:07:20 - (small cross talk)
00:07:28 - Unknown Speaker: uh-huh (inaudible)
00:07:35 - Lena: From a timeline perspective, what's your target for a pilot?
00:07:40 - Dana: We'd like an internal pilot in three weeks to validate egress & DNS flows with our partners. production in Q1 next year.
00:07:49 - Lena: ok that fits. we'll aim to get the runbook and security pack to you in 3 business days. Marcus will follow up on the transit design.
00:07:58 - Marcus: I'll sketch three options: 1) PrivateLink endpoints only (no peering) — simplest DNS but Redwood egress IPs used; 2) VPC peering + route tables — gives more control but need careful route propagation and Route53 resolver for DNS; 3) Transit gateway with Direct Connect — best for on-prem performance and using your NAT egress. I'll include cost/ops tradeoffs.
00:08:21 - Ravi: If we pick option 3, Direct Connect timeframe is longer. do you support a hybrid approach for the pilot?
00:08:28 - Marcus: Absolutely — pilot with PrivateLink and Redwood egress IPs so you can test functionally; later swap to transit/direct connect for full control. we can also add a proxy so your partner sees your IPs for specific routes.
00:08:41 - Elena: Any known limitations with AWS PEERING across accounts and shared services? we use multiple AWS accounts per BU.
00:08:48 - Marcus: Peering is per VPC pair and not transitive. if you have multiple accounts, typical patterns are: a central networking account with Transit Gateway or Route53 resolver endpoints to centralize. PrivateLink can be easier across multiple accounts because interface endpoints can be created in each VPC.
00:09:05 - Dana: We maintain a central NOC that will want to review your runbook. what do you need from us right now to start?
00:09:12 - Lena: The immediate items: VPC CIDRs, desired region(s) and list of partner IPs to be whitelisted. also the email for your security reviewer so we can pass SOC2 and architecture docs.
00:09:24 - Ravi: We'll compile that. one more: do you support IP allowlisting per model or is it per-deployment?
00:09:33 - Marcus: Currently per-deployment by default; we can do per-route or per-model gating but that requires an extra configuration step and is typically part of Dedicated offering. we'll note that as an ask.
00:09:47 - Lena: Noted. I'll also surface options for per-model network policies in the docs.
00:09:54 - (short pause)
00:10:05 - Marcus: Quick technical aside: if you're concerned about source IP preservation for logging, one strategy is to terminate client-side TLS at your side and forward requests through a proxy that appends X-Forwarded-For to the payload. it's more hands-on but gives you full control.
00:10:20 - Ravi: Ok that helps. for the pilot we'd prefer Redwood egress IPs to reduce initial changes.
00:10:25 - Lena: Cool. we'll prepare a minimal IP pool for pilot.
00:10:30 - Elena: Any recommendations on firewall ports? partner said they'll open only 443 and a couple of management ports.
00:10:36 - Marcus: 443 is the primary one; management plane uses a handful of ports which we'll list. typically only outbound 443/8443 for control plane; we avoid opening inbound except for interface endpoints where you control inbound rules.
00:10:51 - Dana: On monitoring—can we get flow logs or packet captures? our security folks love VPC flow logs.
00:10:57 - Marcus: Yes flow logs supported, and audit logs for API calls. packet capture is more ad-hoc but we can enable VPC traffic capture during troubleshooting.
00:11:08 - (time jumps — they dig into a bit more detail)
00:15:02 - Ravi: Quick clarification — PrivateLink DNS records, will they be friendly names like api.redwood.example? we use internal naming conventions.
00:15:10 - Marcus: Yes you can either use our hostnames and map them into your private hosted zone or create CNAMEs to the interface endpoints. we'll provide example CloudFormation to automate this.
00:18:36 - Elena: KMS again — do you keep copies of encryption keys? our policy says keys must be customer-owned.
00:18:45 - Lena: We do a KMS integration where keys are never exported from your KMS; we perform envelope encryption. Redwood doesn't persist raw keys. we'll include the KMS integration details in the security pack.
00:21:10 - Dana: The auditors will need timelines and an architecture diagram. can you produce a sketch for the pilot?
00:21:17 - Marcus: Yes, I'll produce a one-page diagram for pilot with PrivateLink and a second for the transit/direct connect option with estimated cutover steps.
00:22:00 - Lena: Let's capture next steps: I'll send security pack and runbook; Marcus will send diagrams and transit options; Ravi will share CIDRs and partner IPs; we reconvene for a technical deep dive next week.
00:22:12 - Ravi: Sounds good. anything else?
00:22:20 - Dana: no, that covers it. thank you.
00:22:25 - Lena: Thanks everyone. we'll follow up with calendar invites.
00:22:30 - (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription quality: some speaker overlap, a few words dropped (e.g., Privatelink sometimes as private link), proper nouns occasionally mistranscribed.
